subject: Business
title: Authority Bias: Trusting the Expert
description: A micro-lesson that makes Authority Bias: Trusting the Expert usable.

hook.text: Milgram's experiment: ordinary people shocked strangers to dangerous levels because a doctor told them to.

buildup.text: Authority bias means we defer to experts and authority figures, sometimes without questioning them.

discovery.text: Uniforms, titles, and confident tone all trigger obedience — even when the authority is fake.

twist.text: Advertisers use actors in lab coats to sell toothpaste. We know they're actors and it still works.

climax.text: In organizations, junior staff suppress good ideas because a senior leader disagrees.

punchline.text: Credentials impress us. But credentials can be wrong.

quiz.question: What did Milgram's experiment demonstrate?
options: People obey authority figures even against their own moral judgment
Only certain personality types follow orders

details.summary: Authority bias is the tendency to attribute greater accuracy and trustworthiness to the opinions of authority figures regardless of the content. In business, this leads teams to defer to senior leaders or credentialed experts even when their judgments are flawed.
details.whyItMatters: Authority bias suppresses dissent and diverse perspectives in organizations. Teams that blindly follow authority miss errors, reduce innovation, and make worse decisions than those that encourage constructive challenge.
takeaways: People overweight opinions from perceived authorities in decision-making
Milgram's experiments dramatically demonstrated obedience to authority
Flat hierarchy cultures reduce authority bias and improve team decisions

faq.question: How does authority bias affect business meetings?
faq.answer: Junior team members self-censor when senior leaders speak first. Good ideas are dismissed if they come from lower-ranking employees. Having leaders speak last and soliciting input anonymously before discussions helps counter this bias.

faq.question: Is authority bias always harmful in organizations?
faq.answer: Not always. Deferring to genuine expertise in technical matters is often efficient and appropriate. The bias becomes harmful when people defer to authority based on rank or title rather than actual relevant expertise in the specific decision at hand.
